opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think if you look at the history of learning, and at what we know from developmental science, there are really two very different kinds of learning that children are designed to do. In the very early years, from birth to about five or six, children are doing what I think of as exploratory learning. They're like little scientists, playing, experimenting, figuring out how the world works, and they do that without anyone really needing to teach them in a formal way.

But by the time children reach school age, something shifts. What they're designed to do then is to take the skills that the people around them have, and master them, become really proficient at them. And for most of human history, the way that happened was through apprenticeship. You'd watch someone who was skilled, a weaver or a hunter or a cook, and you'd gradually take on more and more of the task yourself, with that person scaffolding you, correcting you, letting you try things.

Now, school as we know it is a very recent invention. It's only been around for a couple of hundred years in its present form, and it was really designed to train people for things like factory work or clerical work. It's oddly disconnected from the way children naturally learn. It tends to emphasize things like test-taking, answering a teacher's question correctly, which isn't really a skill that's useful anywhere except in school.

If you look at the places where school-age children do learn effectively, it's often things that look very much like apprenticeship. Think about kids who learn to play a sport, or a musical instrument, or a video game, or the way kids learn to code by working alongside someone more experienced. There's a model, there's practice, there's a gradual increase in responsibility, and there's a real, meaningful product at the end. The child cares about getting good at the thing itself, not just about getting the grade.

So my view is that if we want schools to work with, rather than against, the way children actually learn, we should look much more closely at that apprenticeship model: real skills, real mastery, learning from people who actually do the thing well. That seems to me much more in keeping with what children have evolved to do at that age.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from early exploratory learning to mastering skills at school age, but does not communicate that the skills are acquired for exploitation.

r002.rationale: It presents apprenticeship as a way to master skills, but does not say children acquire them for later exploitation.

r003.rationale: Sports and music are given as examples of apprenticeship-like learning, but the response does not say children are attracted to them partly because of that learning.

r004.rationale: The response does not use the baseball-games analogy or criticize science education for delaying participation in scientific inquiry.

r005.rationale: It says schools emphasize test-taking and that this skill is useful mainly in school, but does not say children’s practice produces expertise in being students.

r006.rationale: The response does not discuss children’s difficulty devising original experiments or attribute it to a lack of independent practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing to remember is that for most of human history, and really for most of the species that have childhoods at all, the way that you learned the things you needed to know as an adult was by hanging around adults who were actually doing those things. You watched, you imitated, you got to try your hand at a smaller version of the real task, and somebody who was an expert corrected you and gave you a bit more rope as you got better. That's apprenticeship. And it's striking how good children are at that kind of learning. Even a two-year-old is remarkably sensitive to what adults are doing, why they're doing it, whether they're doing it on purpose, and they'll imitate and modify what they see.

Now, the school model that we've had for about 150 years is a very different thing. It's a kind of mass-production system that comes out of the Industrial Revolution, and it was designed to take a lot of children and have them acquire a particular set of skills, mostly reading and writing and arithmetic, that are actually rather unnatural. Those are really the last 5,000 years of human history, and they're skills that nobody in a hunter-gatherer society needed. So you need a somewhat special kind of institution to teach them, and I think that's actually fine for that narrow purpose.

But the trouble is that we've expanded that model to cover all of what it means to be a child and to learn. And the things that children are really good at, that exploratory, play-based, observational learning, get squeezed out. What I would like to see, especially for older children, is something more like the apprenticeship, where you're actually doing the thing with someone who knows how to do it. If you want to learn to be a scientist, the best way is to work in a lab with scientists, not to sit in a lecture memorizing the periodic table. If you want to be a carpenter or a cook or a programmer, same thing. There's good evidence that this is how expertise actually develops, even in the more academic parts of our culture. Graduate school, after all, is really just a medieval apprenticeship system that we've kept around because it works.

The other advantage is motivational. One of the things that happens in school is that children are asked to learn things whose point is entirely deferred, and that's hard for anybody. In an apprenticeship, you can see why you're doing it. The feedback is immediate, it comes from the world rather than from a grade, and you can see yourself getting closer to being the kind of person you'd like to become. That's the way human beings have always learned, and I'm not sure we've improved on it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts exploratory learning with apprenticeship, but does not frame development as a shift toward acquiring skills for exploitation.

r002.rationale: It recommends apprenticeship especially for older children and describes learning practical skills by doing the work alongside experts, with examples such as science, carpentry, cooking, and programming.

r003.rationale: It does not mention children’s attraction to music or sports or connect that attraction to apprenticeship learning.

r004.rationale: It favors working in a lab over lectures for learning science, but does not use the analogy of postponing baseball games.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss children becoming expert students or mastering test-taking through school practice.

r006.rationale: It does not attribute difficulty devising original experiments to a lack of independent practice.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think one of the striking things about children is how much they learn by participating in what other people are doing. In an apprenticeship, you’re doing something that has a purpose, alongside somebody who knows how to do it better than you do. You can watch them, try things yourself, get feedback, and gradually take on more responsibility.

That brings together two things that we sometimes separate in discussions of education: children’s own exploration and learning from other people. An apprentice isn’t just being told facts, but she isn’t being left to discover everything from scratch, either. The expert can structure the situation so that the child can make progress.

And you can see why you’d want to learn. You’re learning mathematics because you need to figure something out, or learning to write because there’s something you want to communicate. That gives the practice and effort a point. I think we could bring much more of that into school, including for quite abstract intellectual work.

r001.rationale: The response combines children’s exploration with learning from others, but does not describe development as a shift toward skills for exploitation.

r002.rationale: It presents apprenticeship as a way to learn skills, but does not identify those skills as ones children will use for exploitation.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss children’s interest in music or sports.

r004.rationale: It does not use baseball games or delayed participation in scientific inquiry as an analogy.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss school practice producing expertise in being a student or taking tests.

r006.rationale: It does not address original experiments or attribute difficulty devising them to lack of independent practice.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one of the striking things about human beings is that children have to learn an enormous amount, and for most of human history they didn’t learn it by sitting in classrooms listening to lectures. They learned by participating in what the people around them were doing. They watched, they tried things, and someone who knew more helped them when they got stuck.

An apprenticeship brings together two things that we sometimes think of as opposites. There’s room for the learner to explore and take initiative, but there’s also a skilled person providing guidance. And you can see what the activity is for. You’re making something or solving a problem, rather than just doing an exercise because somebody told you to.

That doesn’t mean we should send children out to become blacksmiths instead of teaching them mathematics. It means asking how we could make learning mathematics more like participating in mathematics—seeing how someone approaches a problem, trying it yourself, getting feedback, and gradually taking on more responsibility. The important thing is that you’re learning how to do something, including how to think, in the company of people who can do it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions exploration and skill learning, but does not describe development as a shift toward acquiring skills for exploitation.

r002.rationale: It presents apprenticeship as guided, practical learning, but does not say children acquire skills for exploitation.

r004.rationale: It does not use baseball games or delayed participation in scientific inquiry as an analogy.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss school practice producing expertise in test-taking or being a student.

r006.rationale: It does not address students’ ability to devise original experiments or their independent-work practice.
